lead: This unit turns the abstract idea of a continuous-time LTI system into a working tool: find the impulse response h(t), convolve it with the input, and read causality and stability from it. After this unit you can evaluate convolution integrals, solve simple differential-equation systems in the time domain, and write a second-order system in state-variable normal form.
about: The unit starts with the definition of a continuous-time LTI system in 2.1: linearity plus time invariance. Chapter 2.2 measures such a system by two responses, the impulse response h(t) and the step response s(t). Chapter 2.3 uses h(t) in the convolution integral to get the output for any input. Chapter 2.4 collects the algebra of convolution, and 2.5 turns h(t) into tests for causality and BIBO stability. Chapter 2.6 connects the time-domain view to systems written as linear constant-coefficient differential equations, including a first-order RC circuit. Chapter 2.7 rewrites an nth-order equation as first-order state equations in normal form. The thread is one object, h(t), seen as definition, computation, property, test and state model.

chapters.idea: An LTI system is one that obeys superposition and does not change when the input is shifted in time.
chapters.depth: Definition of linearity: T{a x₁+b x₂}=aT{x₁}+bT{x₂}; time invariance: input x(t−τ) gives output y(t−τ). Some syllabi say shift-invariant for time-invariant. Keep to continuous time here; the discrete-time parallel comes in Unit 5. Test a formula with one counterexample for linearity and one for time invariance. Do not derive convolution in this chapter.

figure.title: LTI test
figure.aria: Flowchart tests a system for linearity first, then time invariance; a no at either test gives not LTI, and two yes gives LTI.

chapters.example: Test y(t)=3x(t)+2 for linearity and time invariance. Take x₁(t)=1, x₂(t)=2, a=2, b=3. At t=0, T{2x₁+3x₂}=T{8}=26, but 2T{x₁}+3T{x₂}=2(5)+3(8)=34, so the system is not linear. Take x(t)=t and delay τ=2 s: input x(t−2)=t−2 gives 3(t−2)+2=3t−4; shifted output y(t−2)=3(t−2)+2=3t−4, so it is time-invariant. Result: not LTI.
chapters.trap: A formula with no explicit t need not be time-invariant; y(t)=x(2t) is time-varying. Also an offset such as +2 breaks linearity but not time invariance.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: system properties, linearity, time invariance, impulse and step signals.
chapters.leave: Convolution integral to 2.3; system classification details to Unit 1; Laplace tests to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The impulse response h(t) is the output to δ(t); the step response s(t) is the output to u(t), and the two are related by integration and differentiation.
chapters.depth: Impulse response h(t), also called the weighting function; step response s(t), also called the indicial response. For an LTI system s(t)=∫₋∞ᵗ h(λ)dλ, and h(t)=ds/dt. Use a first-order RC low-pass as the physical example. Keep convolution for 2.3 and differential equations for 2.6.

figure.aria: Normalised impulse response falls from one while the step response rises from zero to one, both plotted against t over the time constant.

chapters.example: An RC low-pass has R=1 kΩ, C=1 μF, so τ=RC=1 ms. Find h(t) and s(t). h(t)=(1/τ)e^{−t/τ}u(t)=1000 e^{−1000t}u(t) s⁻¹. Then s(t)=∫₀ᵗ h(λ)dλ=(1−e^{−t/τ})u(t). At t=1 ms, s=1−e⁻¹=0.632 and h=1000e⁻¹=368 s⁻¹.
chapters.trap: h(t) is not the step response; s(t) is the integral of h(t). Do not drop u(t), and keep the 1/τ factor that carries the unit s⁻¹.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1; Unit 1 standard signals δ(t) and u(t).
chapters.leave: Convolution to 2.3; Laplace transform of h(t) to Unit 4; second-order response details to 2.6.

chapters.idea: For an LTI system the output is the convolution integral y(t)=∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ, evaluated by flipping, shifting, multiplying and integrating.
chapters.depth: Convolution integral, also called the superposition integral. Graphical flip-shift-multiply-integrate method. Limits depend on the overlap of x(τ) and h(t−τ). Work finite-duration inputs as separate time cases; give one short numerical trapezoid-rule check. Do not prove properties here.

figure.aria: Output rises to a peak near t=2 s and then decays, showing the overlap of a two-second rectangle with a decaying exponential.

chapters.example: Let x(t)=u(t)−u(t−2) and h(t)=e^{−t}u(t). Find y(t)=x(t)*h(t). For 0≤t<2, y=∫₀ᵗ e^{−(t−τ)}dτ=1−e^{−t}. For t≥2, y=∫₀² e^{−(t−τ)}dτ=e^{2−t}−e^{−t}. At t=1 s, y=0.632; at t=2 s, y=0.865; at t=3 s, y=0.318.
chapters.trap: The integration limits are where x(τ) and h(t−τ) overlap, not always 0 to t. Flip h(t) to h(−t) first, then shift; do not flip x in the standard formula.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2; Unit 1 shifting and scaling of signals.
chapters.leave: Convolution properties to 2.4; stability and causality tests to 2.5; transform-domain convolution to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Convolution obeys an algebra: order, grouping and distribution can be changed, and δ(t) is the identity.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a named chapter; keep it short. State commutative, associative and distributive laws; identity x*δ=x; shift rule; duration addition for finite-duration signals; differentiation and integration rules. Give one-line substitution proofs, not long derivations.

figure.aria: Convolution of a two-second rectangle with a three-second rectangle gives a trapezoid of total duration five seconds and peak two.

chapters.example: Let x(t)=u(t)−u(t−2), width 2 s, and h(t)=u(t)−u(t−3), width 3 s. Find the duration and peak of y=x*h. The result is y=t for 0≤t≤2, y=2 for 2≤t≤3, and y=5−t for 3≤t≤5, zero otherwise. Duration is 2+3=5 s; peak is 2 on 2≤t≤3.
chapters.trap: Durations add only for finite-duration signals; heights do not add in general. δ(t) is the identity, not zero, and convolution with δ(t−t₀) shifts the signal.
chapters.leave: Long proofs and transform convolution theorems to Unit 3; Laplace-domain multiplication to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A system is causal if h(t)=0 before t=0, and BIBO stable if the area under |h(t)| is finite.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate chapter; keep it to tests on h(t). Causal iff h(t)=0 for t<0. BIBO (bounded-input bounded-output) stable iff ∫|h(t)|dt<∞. Test simple impulse responses; note that finite area and causality are independent. Leave pole tests and Routh tables to Unit 4.

figure.title: Causality and stability tests
figure.aria: Flowchart checks causality from h(t)=0 for negative time, then checks finite area under absolute h; both yes gives causal and stable.

chapters.example: Test h₁(t)=e^{−2t}u(t), h₂(t)=e^{2t}u(−t), and h₃(t)=u(t). For h₁: h₁=0 for t<0, so causal; ∫|h₁|dt=1/2, finite, so stable. For h₂: nonzero for t<0, so not causal; ∫|h₂|dt=1/2, finite, so stable but not causal. For h₃: causal, but ∫|h₃|dt=∞, so not stable.
chapters.trap: Causal does not imply stable; u(t) is the standard counterexample. A signal with finite area can be anti-causal, as h₂ shows. Check the two conditions separately.
chapters.leave: Pole-location and Routh stability tests to Unit 4; discrete-time BIBO to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A continuous-time LTI system can be written as a linear constant-coefficient differential equation whose time-domain solution gives the output.
chapters.depth: Linear constant-coefficient differential equation (LCCDE). Order, characteristic equation, natural and forced response, zero-input and zero-state response, initial conditions. Solve first-order RC and RL, plus one second-order mass-damper; mention transfer function only as a name, not as the method.

figure.aria: Step response of the RC circuit rises from zero and reaches about 0.632 V at one millisecond, then approaches one volt.

chapters.example: A series RC circuit has R=1 kΩ, C=1 μF, input x(t) V and output y(t) V across C. Its equation is RC dy/dt+y=x, with RC=1 ms. With y(0)=0 and x(t)=u(t) V, solve y(t)=(1−e^{−1000t})u(t) V. At t=1 ms, y=0.632 V.
chapters.trap: Initial conditions are on y and its derivatives, not on the input. For RC, the time constant is τ=RC, not R+C, and the zero-input and zero-state parts add.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 standard signals and basic circuit laws; Chapter 2 for h(t).
chapters.leave: Laplace solution and transfer function to Unit 4; state equations to 2.7; higher-order numerical solution to later courses.

chapters.idea: An nth-order differential equation can be split into n first-order state equations in normal form.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. State variables, state vector, state equations x′=Ax+Bu, output y=Cx+Du. Normal form, also called phase-variable or companion form, for an LCCDE. Do a second-order example with a signal-flow block diagram; leave matrix solutions to later.

figure.title: Normal-form state diagram
figure.aria: Signal-flow diagram for y double prime plus three y prime plus two y equals u: input enters a summing node, two integrators produce x2 and y=x1, with feedback gains minus three and minus two.

chapters.example: Write y″+3y′+2y=u(t) in normal state form. Let x₁=y and x₂=y′. Then x₁′=x₂, x₂′=−2x₁−3x₂+u, and y=x₁. In matrix form A=[[0,1],[−2,−3]], B=[0,1]ᵀ, C=[1,0], D=0.
chapters.trap: State choice is not unique, but normal form uses y and its derivatives, not derivatives of the input. Match the sizes of A, B, C and D to the number of states and inputs.
chapters.leave: Solving x′=Ax+Bu with e^{At}, controllability and observability to later control courses; discrete state models to Unit 6.
